items.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: all of them were right in that band. It was a great band, and then I started going, playing with them.

ctx.x: Any other good anecdotes about the bands? Memorable experiences seeing them...

Oh, yeah. When I came back from the Navy, they had an Army base in Greensboro, the O.R.D., Overseas Replacement Depot. I was back at the cottage, and the guys from the Army band used to come over and play with the other band. They hadn’t seen me. Then I came back, and I’m playing bebop. I’m not playing like the guys around Greensboro. The guy said, “Who is this guy? Is this guy from New York?” They said, “No, he’s from here.” They said, “Oh, no, he can’t be from here playing like that.” But see, I had been in the…
Talk about how for you the Ellington band was different.

items.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: that's were I met Lou Donaldson, down there.

ctx.x: So you also played as well as the parades and ceremonial kinds of things and everything. Did you play at dances and various things?

Oh, we played dances, yeah. Uh-huh. [affirmative] Yeah, but they all -- all -- always. Did we ever play? I think we did, yeah. We even played some of the Caucasian dances, too. But -- but we played mostly, you know, over there under the Big Top. You know, that they called it. You know. And, like, it got so that the band -- as a matter of fact, Lou Donaldson [phonetic sp.], that's were I met Lou Donaldson, down there. Lou Donaldson and -- because he was -- he was, I think he was in A&T College, you know. But I met.
